tip: Languages take the definite article in French: comprennent l'espagnol = understand Spanish. English drops the "the," French keeps it.
Adjectives ending in -ent build adverbs in -emment, said like "amman": prudent becomes prudemment = carefully. The double m hides an a-sound.
You don't pay attention in French, you make it: faire attention. Nous faisons attention = we're paying attention. faire covers loads of everyday actions.
French has two "know" verbs. savoir is for facts and info: il sait tout = he knows everything. For people and places you'd switch to connaître.
'Avoir froid' = to be cold (feeling), 'avoir chaud' = to be hot. French says 'I have cold/heat' not 'I am cold/hot'.
'Avoir besoin de' = to need. Literally 'to have need of': j'ai besoin d'eau (I need water).
Payer can be spelled je paye or je paie – both are correct. Verbs ending in -ayer allow both forms.
dépenser is only for spending money or energy, never time. Elle dépense trop = she spends too much (cash). For spending time you'd use passer.
l'addition is the restaurant bill, not a maths sum. Ils partagent l'addition = they split the bill. Say "l'addition, s'il vous plaît" to pay.
Vouloir takes a bare infinitive – no 'to' in between: 'veut partir' is want + leave, straight through. Pouvoir works the same: il peut partir.
encore means "still" here, but also "again" or "more": elle dort encore = she's still asleep. Context picks the meaning.
Ouvrir ends in -ir but conjugates like an -er verb: it's 'j'ouvre', not j'ouvris. Couvrir and offrir do the same.
To cook is literally "to do the kitchen": faire la cuisine. Tu fais la cuisine = you cook. French leans on faire for household chores.
Regarder already means 'look at' – the 'at' is baked in: 'regardez la télévision', never regarder à. Écouter (listen to) works the same way.
'Jouer au' is used for sports (au football), while 'jouer du/de la' is for instruments (du piano). The preposition changes the meaning.
In French, meals take the definite article: 'le dîner' (dinner), 'le déjeuner' (lunch). English drops it; French doesn't.
For things, adorer is 'love' while aimer only reaches 'like': 'adorent le chocolat' is stronger than aiment. (For people, aimer already means love.)

target: Il passe ses vacances à Nice.
english: He spends his holidays in Nice.
tip: Passer is 'to spend' for time, not money: 'passe ses vacances' = spends his holidays. Spending money is dépenser.
French keeps the article for likes in general: 'aimez le café' is literally 'like the coffee', where English just drops the 'the'.
'Porter' means both 'to carry' and 'to wear': context determines. 'Portent des lunettes' = they wear glasses.
changer de takes a bare noun, no article: change de train = change trains. Same pattern in changer d'avis = change your mind.
'Finir de + infinitive' means 'to finish doing something'. This is a common -ir verb construction.
des is the plural "some" and can't be dropped: plantez des fleurs = plant (some) flowers. English omits it, French never does.
'Être en retard' = to be late. French uses the preposition 'en' before 'retard', not 'à' or nothing.
Des is the plural 'some' English usually skips: 'prend des photos' = takes (some) photos. French won't drop it – bare prend photos is wrong.
"Some" before a vowel sound becomes de l', whatever the gender: bois de l'eau = drink (some) water. Before a consonant it splits into du or de la.
'Habiter à' is used with cities: 'habiter à Paris'. For countries, use 'habiter en' (feminine) or 'habiter au' (masculine).
After a preposition French uses stressed pronouns: à toi, not "à te." Je pense à toi = I'm thinking of you. Also pour moi, avec lui.
You "pose" a question in French, not ask it: poser une question. Tu poses une question = you ask a question.
réussir = to pass (succeed at). Careful: passer un examen means only to SIT it, not pass it. Elle réussit son examen = she passes her exam.
